items.title: Astronauts on the ISS are not in zero gravity
items.claim: The International Space Station orbits about 400 km up. Earth's gravity there is still 89 percent of its surface value. Astronauts float not because gravity is absent but because both they and the station are in continual free fall.
items.prompt: If they're falling, why don't they hit Earth?

options.text: The station has engines that hold it up
They are falling — but also moving sideways at about 7.7 km/s, so the curvature of their trajectory matches the curvature of the Earth and they keep missing the ground
Gravity gets cancelled by the Moon
Air pressure at altitude keeps them up

items.reveal_title: Orbit is free fall that misses the Earth
items.reveal:
Newton's thought experiment: fire a cannonball horizontally from a mountaintop. Slow shots fall to Earth. At about 7.9 km/s, the cannonball falls fast enough that the Earth curves away beneath it at the same rate. It never lands — that's orbit.

The ISS is doing this constantly. The astronauts and the floors of the station are all accelerating toward Earth's centre at about 8.7 m/s squared — but in a circular path that misses the Earth.

Inside the station, since everything accelerates equally, nothing presses against anything else. The famous 'microgravity' isn't an absence of gravity — it's the equivalence of free fall and inertial motion that Einstein turned into the equivalence principle of general relativity.
items.why: Pop culture says astronauts are 'in zero gravity'. They're in nearly normal gravity but in continuous free fall. The two feel identical.

items.title: An ambulance's pitch drops as it passes you — and that drop is the Doppler effect
items.claim: An approaching ambulance siren sounds higher-pitched than its 'true' frequency; once it passes, the pitch suddenly drops. The shift is the Doppler effect, and it provides a quantitative way to measure radial velocity.

options.text: The siren plays different notes as it moves

Sound waves emitted by a source moving toward you are compressed (higher frequency, higher pitch); waves from a source moving away are stretched (lower frequency, lower pitch). The shift Δf/f equals v/c_sound
Your ears change sensitivity with movement
The siren only changes pitch in air

items.reveal:
For a source moving with speed v toward a stationary observer, the observed frequency is f_observed = f_source × c / (c - v), where c is the speed of sound. For source moving away, replace minus by plus.

At 30 m/s (a fast vehicle) and 343 m/s (speed of sound), the shift is about ±9 percent — easily heard as a pitch change of around a semitone.

The same effect applies to light. Astronomers measure stellar and galactic radial velocities by Doppler shifts of spectral lines. Most galaxies show redshifted spectra: they are moving away. This is how Hubble (1929) showed the universe is expanding.

Doppler weather radar bounces microwaves off raindrops and measures the frequency shift to find wind speeds at altitude. Police radar guns use the same principle to measure car speeds.
items.why: The Doppler effect is taught as 'pitch changes'. It is a universal feature of any wave and underlies tools from speed cameras to cosmology.

items.title: A bridge tore itself apart from a steady wind
items.claim: On 7 November 1940 the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State collapsed after four months in service. A wind of about 19 m/s set the deck twisting at its torsional natural frequency. Within hours, the oscillation built up to several metres of amplitude and the structure failed.
items.prompt: How can a steady wind cause unbounded oscillation?

options.text: The wind happened to gust at exactly the right frequency
Aeroelastic flutter — the bridge's torsional motion changed the air flow in a way that fed energy back into the same motion at the same frequency, amplifying every cycle
The wind was much stronger than reported

items.reveal:
Driven resonance: a periodic external force at the natural frequency drives the oscillation higher each cycle. The amplitude grows linearly with time (limited by damping).

Aeroelastic flutter is different and more dangerous: the structure's own motion alters the airflow, which then drives the motion at the same frequency. It's a feedback loop where the driving frequency automatically locks to the response frequency. A steady wind suffices.

The Tacoma Narrows deck was an aerodynamically simple H-shape with a high aspect ratio. It was particularly vulnerable to torsional flutter at moderate wind speeds.

London's Millennium Bridge in 2000 had a similar story but with pedestrians instead of wind. Walkers' lateral footfalls synchronised with the bridge's natural side-to-side mode; the crowd unconsciously walked in step and amplified the swaying. The bridge was closed and dampers fitted.
items.why: Resonance is taught as benign (musical instruments). Aeroelastic flutter is its destructive cousin — and engineers must design against it explicitly.
